column4: The sleepers send one member with their silver to seek the purest food and bring provision back to the group, closely matching jointly purchased wholesome food shared from one common store.
The question asks whether extended wealth and children are being mistaken for benefits, directly testing the section's equation of abundant property with perceived khayr.
The answer says they do not understand that wealth and children are not necessarily good things being hastened to them, correcting the owner's judgment of what counts as khayr.
A person promises that if God gives from His bounty he will give charity and be righteous, setting the promised opening of the hand that 9:76 reverses.
Once bounty is given, the recipients become miserly with it and turn away, a compact narrative of good-seeming wealth fastening and closing its new owner.
A secure town receives abundant provision from every place but is ungrateful for God's favors, joining plentiful food to the kenud response and to provision withdrawn.
Owners are commanded to contract with enslaved people seeking freedom and give them from God's wealth, directly reversing the section's master who harms his servant and withholds aid.
Taking charity from their wealth purifies and increases them, making release from the store the means of cleansing the possessor rather than diminishing him.
The expiation feeds ten poor people from the ordinary food of one's household, a concrete table where a household's provision is measured into shared portions.
Had provision been expanded without measure, people would transgress; God sends it in due measure, explaining why abundance is not simply khayr and placing the human hoard under divine apportionment.
The chained offender says that his wealth did not avail him, the confessed collapse of the security imagined by the collector before the binding and withheld-food sequence.
The declaration that neither a man's wealth nor his earnings avail him gives the same verdict against wealth imagined as protection or permanence.
Qarun and his dwelling are swallowed, and no company or self-help can save him; the great store and social strength of 28:76 prove unable to hold their owner up.
When the owners confront their ruined garden they say they have been deprived, turning their plan to deprive the poor in 68:24 into deprivation of themselves.
Property is called a means of support, yet guardians must provide food and clothing from it for dependents; the store exists to sustain a household rather than merely remain in the guardian's fist.
A rich guardian must abstain from an orphan's property, a needy one may take fairly, and matured property must be handed over, setting exact limits against absorbing another's share.
Woe is pronounced upon those who take full measure for themselves; 83:2-3 show the one-way distribution that makes their receiving hand open and giving hand tight.
When receiving by measure from others, the defrauders demand the full amount, specifying the acquisitive half of an unjust common transaction.
When measuring or weighing for others, they diminish the portion, the distributive opposite of the section's fairly divided common food.
The good loan releases wealth while God both constricts and expands provision; the ayah redirects the imagery of contraction and opening from the human fist to divine measure and multiplication.
What is with people perishes while what is with God remains, directly overturning the hoarder's hope that retained wealth can make him permanent.
On the final day neither wealth nor children benefit, removing the collector's outward assets before 26:89 identifies the inward possession that matters.
Only the one who comes with a sound heart succeeds, placing the disclosed condition of the chest where wealth fails in 26:88.
The fire is closed over the wealth-counter; the one who enclosed property is finally himself enclosed.
The instruction that mixing life or property with orphans makes them brothers supplies a communal alternative to consuming orphan wealth into one's own store.
A prosperous people are told to eat their Lord's provision and thank Him, giving the section's large pot its civic form: abundant food received together in gratitude.
The good land loses its abundance because of ingratitude, showing what follows when provision meets the kenud response rather than the gratitude commanded in 34:15.
The one who would not urge feeding the poor has no food except foul discharge, a punitive reversal of the meal he refused to open to another.
Wealth and children are not to inspire admiration because they may become a means of punishment, challenging the assumption that abundant possessions deserve the name good.
Worldly splendor is a test, while the Lord's provision is better and more lasting; apparent property-khayr is measured against enduring provision.
Worldly possessions are temporary enjoyment and adornment, whereas what is with God is better and more lasting, correcting attachment's estimate of retained goods.
Whatever people are given is temporary worldly enjoyment, while what is with God is better and lasting, the same boundary between possession and true khayr.
The person who gives his wealth to purify himself is the open-handed counterpart to the self-satisfied miser later contrasted within the surah.
People are told to spend from property over which they have only been made successors, weakening the absolute ownership imagined by the clenched hand.
After Qarun's fall, his former admirers recognize that God expands and restricts provision and that unbelievers do not prosper, correcting their previous desire for his store.
Whatever khayr people spend returns fully to them, making the same word the object of outward giving rather than inward attachment.
Whatever khayr people send ahead for themselves will be found with God as better and greater in reward, presenting the enduring deposit opposed to counted property.
Wealth and children are described as a trial immediately before the command to spend and guard against inner greed in 64:16.
The repeated warning that wealth and children are a trial marks possessions as a test of the holder rather than an uncomplicated good.
Feeding a poor person is the compensating act for one unable to fast, another concrete transfer of one's food into a vulnerable person's portion.
Feeding sixty poor people is required when emancipation and fasting are impossible, turning atonement into a deliberately large communal provision.
Serving youths circulate cups, pitchers, and a goblet from a flowing drink, another shared-table realization of the section's secondary drinking-vessel sense.
The righteous drink from a cup before the passage praises their feeding of loved food, so the vessel belongs to the same open-table sequence as 76:8.
Abraham notices that the visitors' hands do not reach the offered calf; the same visible relation of hand to common food here signals angelic guests, not miserliness.
Sea catch and its food are made provision for people and travelers, giving the section's traveler-meal detail a direct Qur'anic source of food.
Full measure and weight are commanded and people must not be deprived of their goods, setting fairness around the apportioning action evoked by the common pot and lots.
Believers eat from wholesome provision and give thanks, joining clean source, shared food ethics, and the gratitude attached to the section's great pots.
Messengers are commanded to eat wholesome things and act rightly, reinforcing the section's link between food from a clean source and praiseworthy action.
Moses, a displaced traveler after helping others at the well, declares himself in need of whatever khayr God sends, allowing khayr to be heard as needed provision rather than a possessed store.
One of the women invites Moses so her father may reward his help, moving the needy traveler of 28:24 toward a host household and lawful recompense.
God knows what people conceal, disclose, and hold within breasts; in the same surah, 64:9 names the Day of Gathering when this knowledge governs judgment.
This ayah identifies the subject of the later call as the Blaze, supplying the fire whose calling action in 70:17 reaches the collector of 70:18.
Obligatory alms are apportioned among named recipients including the poor, captives, debtors, and traveler, a formal division of the stored wealth into communal shares.
Wealth spent in God's way is likened to a seed multiplying into many grains, answering the collector's desire for increase with abundance produced by release.
Charity given seeking God's favor is what truly multiplies, relocating increase from the counted private store to the gift.
The question asks who could provide if God withheld His provision, exposing the human withholder's dependence on a provision he never controlled.
Water is divided between the people and the she-camel, each turn attended in order; it is a non-gambling scene of a common resource allotted into known shares.
The she-camel has one drinking share and the people another on a known day, pairing an animal with an explicit rule of communal apportionment.
Each tribe knows its drinking place when water is brought from the rock, a collective provision divided without becoming one person's enclosed supply.
The human being never tires of asking for khayr, showing desire's persistent reach toward what it perceives as good even before possession turns into withholding.
The people are likened to startled donkeys in flight; this may faintly extend the section's contrast between an animal surging away and the camel fixed in place, though wealth is absent.
The donkeys flee from a predator, completing the motion image of 74:50; the link is limited to the section's animal movement contrast.
